subject: mathematics
question_text: In triangle ABC, a, b, c are the position vectors of the vertices A, B and C. Prove that the position vector of the centroid is (1/3)(a + b + c).

mark_split.label: Find the position vector of the midpoint of BC
Name the point G and find AG and AD
Show G lies on the median AD
Show G lies on all three medians

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.66, chapter 6 ADDITION OF VECTORS, Short Answer question 10. Only the question was taken — the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work, see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. METHOD CHOICE RECORDED: the short route is to quote that the centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 and then apply the section formula, but that assumes the very concurrency the word centroid names. The card instead names the candidate point G with position vector (a + b + c)/3 and PROVES it lies on the median AD, then uses the symmetry of the expression in a, b and c to place it on the other two medians as well — so the concurrency is proved rather than borrowed. The 2 : 1 ratio then falls out of AG = (2/3) AD instead of being assumed. Checked a second way by the section formula: the point dividing AD in the ratio 2 : 1 from A has position vector (2 × (b + c)/2 + 1 × a)/3 = (a + b + c)/3, the same answer. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 split rewards the midpoint, the two vectors from A, the statement that G is on the median, and the symmetry argument that makes it the centroid. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern; Addition of Vectors has no Section C slot on the paper, so the unit is SAQ and VSAQ only. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the centroid formula — say which point you name first and what you have to show about it.

steps.label: Find the midpoint of BC
steps.margin_note: First mark. The centroid is defined through the medians, and a median needs the midpoint of a side. Write the midpoint rule out rather than quoting it, since it is one of the two facts the proof rests on.
steps.memory_tip: A median starts at the midpoint of a side, and the midpoint of BC has position vector (b + c)/2.
lines: Let O be the origin, so
OA = a,  OB = b,  OC = c.
Let D be the midpoint of BC.
By the midpoint rule,
OD = (b + c)/2
AD is then the median through A.

recall.must_convey: That D is taken as the midpoint of BC with position vector (b + c)/2, so AD is the median through A.
accept: let D be the midpoint of BC with position vector b plus c over two
the midpoint rule gives the average of the two position vectors
AD is the median from A to the midpoint of BC
D ante BC midpoint, dhani position vector b plus c by two
start with the midpoint of one side

steps.why: The centroid has no formula yet at this stage, but the median does. Building the median first gives the proof something concrete to test the candidate point against.
common_mistakes: Writing OD = b + c and losing the division by 2.
Taking D as the midpoint of AB, which does not give the median through A.

steps.label: Name the point G
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give the expression the question offers a name, G, and then build AG and AD from A. Both must start at A so that they can be compared in the next step.
steps.memory_tip: Name the candidate point G first, then build AG and AD, both starting from A.
lines: Let G be the point with
AG = OG − OA = (a + b + c)/3 − a
AD = OD − OA = (b + c)/2 − a

recall.must_convey: That G is named as the point with position vector (a + b + c)/3, and that AG = (b + c − 2a)/3 and AD = (b + c − 2a)/2.
accept: let G be the point whose position vector is a plus b plus c over three
work out AG and AD both starting from A
AG is b plus c minus two a over three and AD is the same top over two
G ani peru petti, AG and AD rendintini A nunchi build chestam
subtract OA from both to get the two vectors from A
heard_as: a plus b plus c by three
b plus c minus two a

steps.why: The question hands over the answer and asks for a proof, so the honest structure is to name that point and test it. Bringing both vectors to the same top line is what makes the comparison one step long.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the wrong way round, giving AG as a − (a + b + c)/3.
Not putting AG and AD over a common top line, so the multiple is hidden.

steps.label: Show G lies on AD
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The two vectors have the same top line, so one is a plain number times the other. That number, 2/3, both puts G on the median and gives the 2 : 1 ratio.
steps.memory_tip: AG = (2/3) AD. The same fraction that puts G on the median also gives the 2 : 1 ratio.
lines: Comparing the two,
AG = (2/3) AD
AG is a number times AD, and both start
at A, so G lies on the line AD.
Since AG = (2/3) AD, G divides AD with
AG : GD = 2 : 1.

recall.must_convey: That AG = (2/3) AD, so G lies on the median AD and divides it in the ratio 2 : 1 from A.
accept: AG is two thirds of AD so G lies on the median
the two vectors are multiples of each other and share the point A
G divides AD in the ratio two to one from A
AG equals two by three AD, so G median meeda untundi
the ratio AG to GD is two to one

steps.why: Two vectors that are multiples of each other and share a starting point lie along the same line. The fraction 2/3 is a point of the segment, between 0 and 1, so G is inside the median, not on its extension.
common_mistakes: Reading the ratio as 1 : 2 instead of 2 : 1.
Saying only that AG and AD are parallel, without the shared point A.

steps.label: Show G is the centroid
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One median is not enough: the centroid is where all three meet. The expression (a + b + c)/3 treats a, b and c alike, so the same working at B and at C puts G on those medians too.
steps.memory_tip: The expression treats a, b and c alike, so the same working at B and C puts G on all three medians.
lines: The expression (a + b + c)/3 does not change
if the letters a, b, c are swapped.
So the same working with the midpoint of
CA, and with the midpoint of AB, puts G on
the other two medians as well.
G is the common point of the three medians,
which is the centroid of triangle ABC.

recall.must_convey: That the expression is unchanged when a, b, c are swapped, so G lies on all three medians and is therefore the centroid.
accept: the formula treats a b and c the same so the same working puts G on the other medians
G lies on all three medians so it is the centroid
by symmetry the same argument works at B and at C
expression symmetric kabatti moodu medians meeda G untundi
therefore the position vector of the centroid is a plus b plus c by three
heard_as: a plus b plus c by three

steps.why: The centroid is defined as the common point of the three medians, so a point proved to lie on all three is it. The symmetry of the expression saves repeating the same six lines twice.
common_mistakes: Stopping after one median, which only shows G is somewhere on AD.
Assuming the three medians meet at a point instead of showing that G is on each of them.
